title: Fuzzy inference systems for mineral prospectivity modeling-optimized using Monte Carlo simulations
author: Chudasama

steps.title: Rescale input data
steps.instruction: Rescale all input evidence layer values to the range 0–1 before any further processing.

steps.title: Assign initial membership parameters
steps.instruction: Set the initial (expected) parameters of each fuzzy membership function to match the statistics of the training data (Table 1) for mineralized and non‑mineralized drill‑core sections.

steps.title: Define beta‑PERT bounds
steps.instruction: For every membership‑function parameter, define a beta‑PERT distribution using the minimum = first quartile (Q1) and maximum = third quartile (Q3) values from Table 1, and the mode = the expected value assigned in the previous step.

steps.title: Monte Carlo sampling
steps.instruction: Randomly draw 1 000 samples from each beta‑PERT distribution to generate a set of possible parameter values for every linguistic term.

steps.title: Compute fuzzy memberships
steps.instruction: For each sampled parameter set, calculate the corresponding fuzzy membership values for the associated linguistic fuzzy set.

steps.title: Build membership value distribution
steps.instruction: Collect all computed membership values to form a probability distribution for each linguistic term (Fig. 1c).

steps.title: Extract certainty envelope
steps.instruction: From the membership‑value distribution, determine the 90 % certainty envelope and extract the 10th, 50th (median) and 90th percentiles.

steps.title: Create confidence‑level membership functions
steps.instruction: Use the 10‑percentile, median and 90‑percentile values as the parameters of three separate membership functions representing 10 % confidence (most conservative), expected (most probable) and 90 % confidence (most optimistic) levels.

steps.title: Repeat for all linguistic values
steps.instruction: Apply steps 2‑8 to every linguistic value in all evidence layers (total 17 linguistic values across 7 evidence layers, as listed in Table 2).

steps.title: Construct FIS rule base
steps.instruction: Build the Mamdani‑type fuzzy inference system by combining the linguistic inputs with IF‑THEN rules, aggregating the rule outputs, and defuzzifying to obtain crisp prospectivity values.

substeps.instruction: Fuzzify each rescaled input using the confidence‑level membership functions.
Apply the predefined IF‑THEN rule set (Fig. 3 and Fig. 4).
Aggregate the consequent fuzzy sets across all rules.
Defuzzify the aggregated output (e.g., centroid method) to produce a prospectivity score.

steps.title: Generate prospectivity maps
steps.instruction: Map the crisp prospectivity scores from each confidence‑level FIS (10 %, expected, 90 %) to produce three prospectivity maps (Fig. 5).

steps.title: Validate model performance
steps.instruction: Assess each FIS using receiver‑operating‑characteristic (ROC) curves, record the area‑under‑curve (AUC) values (0.839 for expected, 0.710 for 10 % confidence, 0.811 for 90 % confidence), and compute capture efficiency (e.g., 80 % of mineralized drill‑core points captured in 24 % of the study area).

description: The FISs at varying confidence levels were derived from the 90-, 50-, and 10- percentile values of the parameters extracted from the 90% certainty envelope of probability distribution of the simulations. The consequent changes in the fuzzy membership values can be visualized for instance in Fig. 2 that shows the fuzzy membership function expected from data statistics and the supplementary membership functions at 10 and 90% confidence levels for the fuzzy set representing ‘mineralized anomalies’ in the evidence layer of NE-SW trending magnetic response. An input value attains three fuzzy membership values, one from each of the confidence levels functions. For instance, an input value 0.218 (around the peak of all the three membership functions) is mapped to nearly maximum membership value (i.e., ∼1) at 10%-, expected, and 90%- confidence levels. However, the differences in the membership values increase towards the tail of the functions, thus indicating progressive increase of the uncertainties. Additionally, for the given example, these differences are not symmetric along both the sides of the curves. For an input value of 0.25, that plots on the right-side curves, the membership values at 10%-, expected, and 90%- confidence levels are 0.825, 0.658, and 0.525, respectively. The right side of the curve shows less difference between the expected and 90%- confidence level membership values. Similarly, for an input value of 0.18, that plots on the left-side curves, the membership values at 10%-, expected and 90%- confidence levels are 0.725, 0.658, and 0.458, respectively. The left-side of the curves show relatively less differences between the expected and 10% confidence level membership values, particularly for values above the inflection points. The same input value, therefore, gets mapped to different output space at varying confidence levels. In Figs. 3 and 4, an input feature vector with values 0.5 in all input variables has the host potential as 0.1, 0.07 and 0.0
